title: Current Use of Sclerotherapy in Italy:  Data Report from Sclerotherapy Survey
content:
Background/Objectives: Sclerotherapy is a common, minimally invasive, outpatient procedure used to treat varicose and spider veins. However, there is significant variability in its practice with regard to techniques, sclerosant types and concentrations, and treatment protocols. The aim of this survey was to collect up-to-date, real-world data on how sclerotherapy is performed in everyday clinical practice in Italy.
Methods: A total of 120 Italian general and vascular surgeons, phlebologists, angiologists, and primary care physicians participated in the Sclerotherapy Survey. The collected data included years of practice, types and concentrations of sclerosing agents used, preparation methods, associated medical treatments, use of auxiliary medical devices, prophylactic anticoagulation, compression therapy, walking after the procedure, and follow-up duration.
Results: Responses showed wide variability among clinicians in their choice of sclerosing agents, concentrations, and preparation methods. The most common practices involved the use of detergent sclerosants, foam preparation using the Tessari method, and the constant use of post-treatment compression. Compression therapy and early mobilization protocols, which are key to optimizing outcomes and reducing complications, were widely adopted. Although there was no uniformity in the responses, antithrombotic prophylaxis was prescribed in select cases. Regarding medical treatments associated with sclerotherapy, a wide variability is observed in the recommendation of drugs or dietary supplements; although there is a growing interest in strategies aimed at improving endothelial function and reducing post-treatment symptoms, prescribing behaviour is not uniform and often tends toward choices that are not supported by established evidence in the literature.
Conclusions: In summary, this survey provides a picture of the current state of the art of sclerotherapy for Chronic Venous Disease in Italy. Overall, the findings highlight the variability of therapeutic approaches based on clinicians’ personal experience and preferences. There is clearly a need for more uniform, standardized, and evidence-based practices. These practices should focus not only on procedural techniques, but also on pharmacological therapies targeting the pathogenic mechanisms of chronic venous disease.
